tasks.prompt: Order a utility wide I/I strategy for the next ten years.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the utility serves 240000 people across 18 sewersheds, wet weather overflows persist, and senior leadership must set one strategy.

cards.label: Rank sewersheds by wet weather peaking, overflow consequence, and cost of removal so effort follows risk and return
Set the ten year funding and delivery profile so study, removal, and capacity work stay in step year by year
Set the strategy outcomes in measurable terms, including peak wet weather flow, overflow frequency, and basement backup risk by sewershed
Define the annual strategy review that compares flow removed with forecast and resets priorities when results differ
Build the utility wide flow picture from permanent meters, lift station records, and past basin studies on one common basis
Choose the strategy mix per sewershed tier, from aggressive source removal to containment to capacity, with reasons recorded

tasks.explanation: Outcomes and a common flow picture come first so every later choice is comparable. The annual review keeps a ten year strategy honest, because removal performance rarely matches the first forecast.

tasks.prompt: Order the decision to move from basin studies to a funded I/I removal program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: six basin studies are complete, removal estimates vary widely, and council funding must be requested this budget cycle.

cards.label: Price the program with given unit rates and stage it so early basins prove effectiveness before later funding is released
Confirm the study evidence is comparable across basins, with the same storm basis, metering period, and source inventory method
Release later stages only when remeasured flow in the early basins confirms the removal the forecast promised
Test the removal forecast with a low effectiveness case so the funding request does not depend on the best outcome
Present the funding case with flow removed, overflow risk reduced, and the capacity spending the program defers
Convert the findings into removable flow by source type, separating public side, private side, and manhole sources

tasks.explanation: Comparable evidence and a low effectiveness case protect the funding decision. Staged release tied to remeasurement means council pays for proven removal, not for study optimism.

tasks.prompt: Order a portfolio review when I/I removal costs rise across the utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: unit costs for lining, grouting, and private side repairs have risen for two years and the removal program is over budget.

cards.label: Rebuild the remaining program cost from current unit rates and the sources actually left in each basin
Reset the program baseline and report the change to the board so future variances are measured against the new basis
Re rank the remaining basins on cost per unit of peak flow removed using the rebuilt costs
Freeze new commitments except work already contracted while the portfolio is reviewed, and record what is paused
Separate cost growth caused by price increases from growth caused by scope added after the original estimates
Recommend whether to re fund, rescope, or stop the lowest return basins, with the residual wet weather risk stated for each

tasks.explanation: Pausing new commitments stops spending on a stale baseline. Separating price growth from scope growth matters because they need different answers, and a reset baseline restores honest variance reporting.

tasks.prompt: Order the setting of a utility wet weather level of service.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. tasks.configuration: Scope: leadership must define what wet weather performance the utility will fund, including the storm size the system should pass without surcharging.

cards.label: Adopt one level of service and translate it into design standards, I/I targets, and capacity triggers for every program
Model or estimate the cost and residual risk of each candidate level using given rates and past storm records
Define candidate service levels in plain terms, such as the design storm passed without surcharge and the overflow frequency accepted
Consult the board on the trade off between rates, risk, and service level before a level is adopted
Describe current performance honestly, including surcharge frequency, overflow locations, and backup history by area
Review performance against the adopted level after each major storm season and report gaps with funded responses

tasks.explanation: A level of service turns wet weather arguments into a funded standard. Adopting it before setting program targets prevents each project from quietly designing to a different storm.

tasks.prompt: Order a private side I/I policy decision at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: basin data show private sources are 55 percent of wet weather inflow, and the utility has no consistent private side policy.

cards.label: Roll out the adopted policy basin by basin with flow remeasurement so its effect is proven, not assumed
Review the legal and equity considerations, including access rights, owner costs, and support for low income households
Recommend the policy to the board with the pilot evidence, the enforcement approach, and the assistance program included
Design policy options, from voluntary incentives to requirements at sale or renovation, with participation forecasts for each
Pilot the leading option in two neighbourhoods and measure participation, cost per property, and flow response
Quantify the private side share by neighbourhood type so the policy is sized to the real source, not an assumption

tasks.explanation: Private side flow cannot be removed by public works alone, so participation evidence drives the policy. Piloting first shows whether owners will act before the utility commits to a citywide rule.

tasks.prompt: Order the response when a completed I/I basin shows little flow reduction.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a flagship basin was declared complete last year, but remeasurement in similar storms shows only a third of the promised reduction.

cards.label: Verify the remeasurement first, checking meter calibration, rain gauge placement, and storm comparability before questioning the work
Diagnose the gap as measurement error, incomplete removal, failed repairs, or an optimistic original estimate, with evidence for each
Report the finding and the correction openly to the board so program credibility rests on verified flow, not claims
Reconcile the source inventory actually removed against the inventory the forecast assumed would be removed
Decide the corrective action, from targeted rework to revised forecasts for all remaining basins using the same method
Inspect a sample of completed repairs for failure, including liner defects, unsealed laterals, and reconnected roof leaders

tasks.explanation: Measurement is checked before work is blamed, because a bad meter can condemn good repairs. Revising forecasts for remaining basins is essential when the method itself proved optimistic.

tasks.prompt: Order a regional I/I coordination plan with neighbouring municipalities.

cards.label: Set a joint I/I reduction commitment per party with milestones that match the shared capacity need date
Set the dispute and review process for years when a party falls behind, including the capacity consequences that follow
Allocate current wet weather flow and remaining capacity among the parties from the shared data, not from estimates
Create a joint annual report that shows each party progress against its commitment and the shared capacity position
Agree the shared flow basis, including meter locations, storm definitions, and how each party reports wet weather peaking
Agree cost sharing for joint metering, studies, and any shared containment or capacity work

tasks.explanation: Shared capacity only works on shared data. A joint annual report with consequences for falling behind is what turns coordination from goodwill into a plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the long term I/I funding strategy linked to rates.

tasks.configuration: Scope: the removal program needs steady funding for fifteen years, and leadership must show how rates support it without sudden increases.

Establish the fifteen year removal need in annual work quantities from the ranked basin program, not as a single lump sum
Show the board the cost of delay, including overflow risk carried longer and capacity work that delay would force
Review the envelope every three years against measured removal and reset the rate path if performance differs
Model rate paths that fund the program, comparing steady small increases with deferred larger increases and their risks
Convert the quantities to annual cost with given unit rates and a stated allowance for price escalation

tasks.explanation: Steady funding matches the steady nature of source removal. Reporting flow removed per dollar each year is the discipline that keeps a fifteen year envelope defensible.

tasks.prompt: Order an I/I strategy for a fast growing service area.

Inspect a sample of new connections during the build out years and correct defects while builders are still responsible
Design the monitoring points into the new network so baseline dry weather flow is known from the first year
Set tight construction standards for the new area, including gasketed joints, tested manholes, and no foundation drain connections to sanitary sewers
Report growth area performance separately so good new construction is not hidden inside poor older basin results
Set the growth area I/I allowance in the capacity plan and track actual peaking against it as connections are added

tasks.explanation: Prevention in new areas is far cheaper than removal later. Separate reporting protects the lesson, because mixing new and old basins hides whether standards are working.

tasks.prompt: Order the close out and lessons review of a ten year I/I program.

Identify methods and source types that underperformed and the evidence that should have flagged them earlier
Assemble the full record, including baseline flows, work completed by basin, spending, and remeasured flows in comparable storms
Report the close out to the board with the verified system peak flow change over the ten years
Score each basin and method on flow removed per dollar and on how long the removal has lasted
Archive the basin data in the asset system so the successor program starts from evidence, not from memory

tasks.explanation: Close out on verified flow change is the only honest score for a decade of spending. Filing the data where the next program works prevents the successor from repeating paid for mistakes.

tasks.prompt: Order the long term cold climate adaptation review for the collection utility.

Prioritize the adaptations by risk, from design standards and station protection to melt response and staffing patterns
Assemble the evidence of change from the utility own records, including freeze events, melt surges, and rain on snow responses by decade
Set the indicators that will show whether the adaptations are working, including freeze calls and melt surcharge frequency
Test current standards and procedures against the changed patterns and list where they no longer fit
Review the adaptation position every five years against the indicators and the updated climate record

tasks.explanation: Adaptation grounded in the utility own records survives scrutiny that generic claims do not. Indicators chosen in advance are what separate an adaptation program from a statement of concern.

tasks.prompt: Order the governance design for a utility scale CMOM program.

Fund the corrective actions the reviews identify through a named budget line so findings do not die unfunded
Define the program purpose and scope in one document, covering capacity assurance, management, operations, and maintenance elements
Publish the program status annually to the board, including measures off target and the actions underway
Assign a senior owner for the program and an owner for each element, with authority to require corrective action
Establish the management review cycle, with quarterly element reviews and one annual program review chaired by senior leadership

tasks.explanation: Named owners with authority separate a program from a binder. A named budget line for corrective actions is the step most often missed, and without it reviews produce lists, not change.

tasks.prompt: Order a CMOM corrective action after repeated overflows at one location.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Compile the full event history for the location, including flows, weather, causes found, and actions taken each time
Close the action only with verification evidence filed, and add the location to the watch list for the next two storm seasons
Assign a corrective action owner at senior level with a funded scope and a completion date
Deliver the lasting fix and verify it in comparable wet weather before the action is closed
Determine the root cause with field evidence, separating capacity limits, blockage patterns, and structural defects

tasks.explanation: Repeated cleanup without root cause work is how known overflow points persist. Closure on verified performance in comparable weather, not on work completion, is the CMOM discipline.

tasks.prompt: Order the annual CMOM report to the board.

File the report and board decisions in the program record so next year review starts from what was promised
State the forward risk plainly, including capacity limits approaching and the assets in poorest condition
Pull the year data from overflow, work order, inspection, and capacity records and reconcile conflicts between sources
Explain every measure off target with its cause and the funded corrective action, owner, and date
Request the specific decisions and funding the board must make, each tied to the risk it addresses

tasks.explanation: Five year trends stop one good or bad year from distorting the account. Tying each funding request to a named risk is what lets a board decide instead of defer.

tasks.prompt: Order a CMOM audit response after an external review finds weak documentation.

Redesign the weakest record steps to be completed at the work site as part of the job, not after it

Set a records quality check, with a monthly sample reviewed by a supervisor and errors fed back to crews
Accept or rebut each finding in writing with evidence, so the response is a record, not an argument
Keep the finding open in the program tracker until the re audit shows sustained improvement

tasks.explanation: Records fail for system reasons more often than for carelessness, so the fix redesigns the step. Keeping the finding open until a re audit proves improvement prevents paper closure.

tasks.prompt: Order the integration of CMOM with the utility safety program.

Fund the safety gaps the review finds through the program budget, with owners and dates like any corrective action
Add safety measures to the CMOM dashboard, including entry permit completion, gas monitor calibration, and near miss reports
Review incidents and near misses in the quarterly CMOM review with the same standing as overflow measures
List the high risk collection tasks inside each CMOM element, including entry, jetting, and bypass pumping work

tasks.prompt: Order a management of change process for collection system modifications.

Sample completed changes each quarter to confirm records match the field, and correct mismatches as findings
Require a simple change record before the change, stating the reason, the risk, and who approves it at the right level
Review temporary changes on a set date so they are removed, made permanent properly, or formally extended
Update drawings, procedures, and the asset register as part of the change, not as a later cleanup

tasks.prompt: Order the CMOM response to a rising basement backup trend.

Map the confirmed backups against surcharge records, pipe condition, and wet weather timing to find the pattern
Track backup rate as a headline CMOM measure with a reduction target and quarterly reporting to leadership
Validate the trend from the records, separating true main surcharge backups from private plumbing failures
Assign corrective actions by cause, which may include cleaning, repair, capacity work, or backwater valve advice to owners

tasks.explanation: Separating private failures from main surcharge is essential, because the fixes and the responsibilities differ. Plain language to affected residents is part of the corrective action, not public relations after it.

tasks.prompt: Order the setting of CMOM performance targets for the next three years.

tasks.configuration: Scope: leadership must set targets for overflows, backups, inspection coverage, and cleaning completion that crews can actually deliver.

Agree the targets with operations leadership and record the resourcing assumptions behind each one
Reset targets only at the annual review, with the reason recorded, so in year misses are managed rather than erased
Set targets that stretch performance without inviting record gaming, and define each measure so it cannot be met by reclassification
Check what the targets would require in crews, equipment, and funding before proposing them

tasks.prompt: Order a CMOM knowledge and succession plan for senior collection roles.

Confirm coverage for every critical task on every shift before the retirements take effect
Pair each retiring operator with a successor on live work, including storm response and station troubleshooting
Identify the critical knowledge at risk, including problem locations, station quirks, and informal workarounds in use
Review the plan at each quarterly CMOM meeting until all critical knowledge has a named backup holder
Test successors by having them lead real tasks while the senior operator observes and corrects

tasks.explanation: Knowledge held only by individuals is an operational risk with a known date. Testing successors on live work proves transfer in a way shadowing alone never does.

tasks.prompt: Order the escalation when CMOM measures miss targets for two quarters.

Review recovery monthly until the measures return to the target path for two consecutive months
Require the element owner to present the cause, separating workload, staffing, equipment, and weather effects with data
Record the episode and its cause in the annual program review so target setting learns from it

tasks.explanation: Two missed quarters is a management signal, not a reporting item. Escalating outside the program matters because the resources to recover usually sit outside it too.

tasks.prompt: Order a twenty year capital plan for the collection network.

Build the need from the asset register, condition grades, remaining life estimates, and capacity triggers, not from last year spending
Adopt the plan with a five year detailed program inside it and an annual update that rolls the detail forward
Separate the plan into renewal, growth capacity, and wet weather programs so each can be judged on its own evidence
Cost each phase with given unit rates and show the annual funding profile the plan requires

tasks.explanation: A twenty year plan built from condition and triggers can be defended asset by asset. Showing backlog trend at lower funding turns a budget cut into an explicit risk decision.

tasks.prompt: Order the renewal funding decision when the backlog is growing.

Identify the renewal rate that holds the backlog steady and the higher rate that reduces it over a stated period
Adopt a funded renewal rate and set the backlog measure as a reported board indicator
Project the backlog and failure risk over ten years at current funding, including overflow and collapse consequences

tasks.explanation: A growing backlog is a slow emergency that annual budgets hide. Making the backlog itself a board indicator keeps the long term visible inside short term decisions.

tasks.prompt: Order the prioritization of capital projects when requests exceed funding.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: project requests total three times the available capital, and departments have scored their own projects favourably.

cards.label: Require every submission on the same evidence format, with condition data, failure history, and cost on given rates
Publish the deferred list with its risks to the board so deferral is a recorded decision, not a quiet omission
Draw the funding line and name the risk accepted for each project deferred below it
Issue one scoring method in advance, covering failure likelihood, consequence, regulatory risk, and coordination value
Score projects in a joint session with operations, engineering, and finance, recording disagreements rather than hiding them
Confirm the funded program can actually be delivered with available design and contractor capacity

tasks.explanation: One method and one format make unlike projects comparable. Naming the risk accepted for each deferral is the step that makes the funding line honest.

tasks.prompt: Order a level of service and asset performance framework for council.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: council wants to know what service the collection assets provide and what condition they must be kept in to sustain it.

cards.label: Have council adopt the service levels, accepting that the adopted levels set the funding requirement
Measure current performance and condition against the framework and identify where service is already below standard
Link each service level to the asset condition and capacity needed to deliver it
Cost the work needed to hold or raise each service level using given unit rates
Define service levels in customer terms, including backup risk, overflow frequency, and response times by area
Report performance and condition against the framework every year in the same format

tasks.explanation: Service levels adopted by council make funding a consequence, not an argument. Reporting in the same format each year is what lets trends, not anecdotes, drive the debate.

tasks.prompt: Order the handover of new subdivision sewers into the asset register.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: rapid growth adds many kilometres of new sewer each year, and several past subdivisions entered service with incomplete records.

cards.label: Audit a sample of past handovers and recover or repair the record gaps found before they become failures
Inspect and test each phase before acceptance and list deficiencies with correction dates for the developer
Start the warranty and inspection clock at acceptance and schedule the first condition check before warranty expiry
Refuse assumption of any reach whose records or condition fail the standard, and record the refusal reasons
Load accepted assets into the register with material, age, depth, and condition at acceptance on the day of handover
Set the acceptance standard in advance, including CCTV evidence, test results, drawings, and asset data in the utility format

tasks.explanation: Assets accepted without records become unknown liabilities for decades. Loading data on the day of handover, and auditing past gaps, protects the register the whole capital plan depends on.

tasks.prompt: Order a capital delivery review after a year of project slippage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: only 60 percent of the planned renewal length was delivered last year, although the budget was largely spent.

cards.label: Reconcile planned against delivered work project by project, separating design delay, procurement delay, and construction problems
Reset the delivery plan with realistic production rates proven by the last two years, not hoped for rates
Track delivery monthly against the reset plan and escalate variance early while correction is still possible
Compare unit costs achieved with the given rates used in planning and identify where estimating was wrong
Report the slippage and the reset to the board with the effect on the backlog measure stated
Check whether scope added during delivery displaced the renewal length the program promised

tasks.explanation: Spending the budget is not delivering the program. Resetting to proven production rates is uncomfortable but is the only basis a board can rely on.

tasks.prompt: Order the decision to renew or rehabilitate a deteriorated trunk sewer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a 1200 mm trunk sewer shows advanced corrosion, it carries half the city flow, and failure would overflow to a river.

cards.label: Assess the consequence of failure during each option, including bypass needs and the environmental harm of a collapse
Plan the chosen work with bypass capacity for peak wet weather flow and a storm contingency before tender
Estimate remaining life under each option, including lining, segmental repair, and full renewal, with the evidence stated
Recommend the option to the board with the failure risk during construction and the service life bought by each choice
Confirm the condition with a full inspection suited to a large live sewer, including wall loss measurement where access allows
Compare whole life cost with given rates, including the risk cost of the shorter lived options

tasks.explanation: On a trunk carrying half the city, consequence dominates the comparison. Bypass sized for wet weather peaks, not averages, is what keeps the cure from causing the overflow it prevents.

tasks.prompt: Order an asset data quality improvement program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: planning is undermined by missing ages, wrong materials, and unmapped reaches in the asset register.

cards.label: Assign a data owner who reports register quality on the same cycle as the capital plan update
Sample the register against field and drawing records to measure the true error rate by data field
Set data standards and checks at every entry point, including capital handovers and repair records, so errors stop entering
Re sample after one year and report the error rate change before expanding the correction scope
Correct the highest value fields first through drawing review, inspection records, and targeted field checks
Rank the fields by planning damage, with condition, material, and connectivity usually ahead of minor attributes

tasks.explanation: Measuring the error rate first prevents a vague cleanup that never ends. Fixing entry points matters more than correcting history, because otherwise the register decays as fast as it is repaired.

tasks.prompt: Order the long term plan for manhole assets across the utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the utility owns 28000 manholes, inspection has covered a third of them, and failures and inflow are concentrated in older areas.

cards.label: Set inspection cycles by risk, with low lying, river valley, and known inflow areas inspected more often than dry upland areas
Track structures rehabilitated and the flow or defect trend in completed basins as the program measures
Group defects by repair type and package work by basin so inflow removal can be measured after each package
Consolidate what is known, including inspection grades, inflow evidence, and failure and odour complaint history by area
Review cycle lengths after the first full round and adjust them to the deterioration rates actually observed
Fund the program as a steady annual quantity rather than occasional projects, matching crew and contractor capacity

tasks.explanation: Risk based cycles spend inspection effort where water and failure concentrate. Steady annual quantities suit manhole work, which is many small repairs rather than a few large projects.

tasks.prompt: Order the disposal and decommissioning of a redundant sewer reach.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a diversion has made one old reach redundant, it still receives some connections, and leaving it live creates collapse and inflow risk.

cards.label: Seal the reach at every connection point to the live system so it cannot admit groundwater or surface water
Decide the decommissioning method per section, from grout filling to removal where future excavation is likely
Confirm every live connection on the reach by records, dye testing, and property checks before any closure is planned
Update the asset register, maps, and flow model so the reach shows as decommissioned everywhere it appears
Transfer or reconnect each live service to the active system and verify flow from each property after transfer
Record the residual risk and inspection need for any section left in the ground, with an owner assigned

tasks.explanation: A redundant sewer is only redundant when every connection is proven moved. Updating every record matters because a reach forgotten on a map will be designed around as if it still carried flow.

tasks.prompt: Order a thirty year capacity strategy for the collection system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: population is forecast to grow 40 percent in thirty years, and leadership must set the capacity path before development commits the system.

cards.label: List the response options per limit, including I/I removal, storage, upsizing, and development phasing, with trigger dates
Adopt the strategy with the board, including the growth assumptions it rests on and the review cycle
Build the flow forecast from approved growth plans, per capita flows, and measured wet weather peaking by sewershed
Revisit the strategy every five years or when growth differs materially from the forecast, and record the changes
Identify when each trunk, lift station, and treatment interface reaches its capacity limit under the forecast
Sequence the responses so long lead items start early enough and short lead items are not built before they are needed

tasks.explanation: Capacity strategy is mostly about timing, because building early wastes capital and building late creates overflows. A five year revisit tied to actual growth keeps the path real.

tasks.prompt: Order the capacity assessment for a proposed major development.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a developer proposes 8000 homes plus commercial space draining to one sewershed with limited spare capacity.

cards.label: Set phasing conditions so occupancy follows the capacity work, with the trigger for each phase stated in the approval
Calculate the added dry and wet weather flows with given per unit rates and the peaking factors used in the capacity plan
Add the approved flows to the capacity ledger so the next proposal is judged against what remains, not what existed
Identify the first element that fails and the number of homes that can be served before it does
Assign the cost of growth driven work under the utility funding policy and record who pays for each element
Check capacity at every element in the path, including local sewers, trunk reaches, the lift station, and the force main

tasks.explanation: Checking every element prevents approving homes that a downstream station cannot serve. The capacity ledger is the control that stops cumulative approvals from silently exceeding the system.

tasks.prompt: Order the response when measured growth outpaces the capacity forecast.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: connections and flows have grown 15 percent faster than forecast for three years, and two capacity triggers will arrive early.

cards.label: Re forecast the affected sewersheds with the observed growth rate and find the new trigger dates
Shorten the strategy review cycle for the affected sheds until growth returns to the forecast band
Apply interim controls, including development phasing advice and intensified I/I removal in the affected sheds
Confirm the variance from metered flows and connection records, separating real growth from I/I change and metering error
Advance the design of the capacity work whose trigger moved most, before construction timing becomes critical
Report the change to the board with the funding profile effect of bringing work forward

tasks.explanation: Early triggers compress design and funding timelines, so advancing design is the first move. Interim I/I removal buys real capacity while the larger work is prepared.

tasks.prompt: Order a wet weather storage strategy for an overflow prone sewershed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: source removal alone cannot meet the adopted service level in one sewershed, and offline storage is proposed to shave storm peaks.

cards.label: Fund construction with the monitoring that will prove the overflow reduction achieved
Size the facility for the adopted level of service and state the larger storms in which overflow will still occur
Compare storage locations on hydraulics, land, odour risk, and the cost of returning stored flow for treatment
Design the operating rules, including fill triggers, drawdown time, cleaning, and odour control after each event
Quantify the storage need from storm records, including the volume above the pass forward capacity for the design events
Review performance after each season and adjust operating rules before considering added volume

tasks.explanation: Storage sized from storm records, with its limits stated, is an honest tool. Operating rules and cleaning decide whether a tank controls overflows or becomes an odour problem.

tasks.prompt: Order the trunk sewer capacity study for the oldest part of the city.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the old core has combined era construction in places, chronic surcharging, and redevelopment pressure adding flow.

cards.label: Set level monitors permanently at the key bottlenecks so the program effect and future growth are visible
Monitor flows and levels through a wet season at the constrictions residents and records identify
Recommend a staged program that matches redevelopment timing so capacity work and growth pay their shares
Build the capacity picture reach by reach, naming each bottleneck and the flow at which surcharging starts
Evaluate options per bottleneck, including relief sewers, storage, I/I removal, and redevelopment conditions
Assemble the record, including original design data where it exists, past surcharge reports, and redevelopment proposals

tasks.explanation: Old core capacity is a chain of bottlenecks, not one number. Permanent monitors at those points turn the study from a snapshot into ongoing capacity management.

tasks.prompt: Order the integration of climate trends into capacity planning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: storm records show more intense short rainfall than the design basis assumed, and leadership must decide how planning responds.

cards.label: Analyse the local storm record honestly, comparing recent intensity and frequency with the period the design storms came from
Apply the revised basis to new designs and to the ranking of capacity and I/I work, not retroactively to every asset at once
Review the storm basis on a fixed cycle so planning follows evidence rather than a single memorable storm
Test the current system against the updated storm basis and list where the service level would no longer be met
Phase the added work into the capital plan with its rate effect shown separately from growth driven work
Set a revised planning basis with the board, stating the storms the utility will design for and the risk accepted beyond them

tasks.explanation: A revised basis adopted openly replaces quiet underdesign. Phasing and separate reporting keep climate driven cost distinct from growth cost, which the board needs to see.

tasks.prompt: Order a capacity ledger and allocation system for all sewersheds.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: approvals are granted shed by shed with no central record, and staff cannot state the remaining capacity in any shed with confidence.

cards.label: Set the allocation rule, including the reserve held for infill, error, and wet weather variability
Audit the ledger annually against metered flows and correct the balances where measurement disagrees
Enter all existing commitments, including approved but unbuilt development, against each shed balance
Publish shed balances to planning staff and developers on a set cycle so expectations match reality
Define capacity per shed from the limiting element, stated as flow and as equivalent homes using given conversion rates
Require every new approval to draw down the ledger at approval, not at connection, so the balance is always current

tasks.explanation: Allocating at approval rather than connection is the rule that prevents overcommitment. The annual audit against metered flow keeps the ledger an engineering record, not an administrative fiction.

tasks.prompt: Order the evaluation of servicing an annexed area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the city has annexed a rural area of 4000 people on septic systems, and council asks whether and how to extend sanitary service.

cards.label: Recommend a servicing and phasing plan with the funding model, including what existing residents are asked to contribute
Survey the existing servicing state, including septic failure evidence, lot sizes, and any surface water quality concerns
Cost each option with given rates, including the operating cost of any new station over its life, not only construction
If servicing proceeds, set construction and connection standards so the new area does not import an I/I problem
Compare servicing options, including gravity extension, a new lift station, and phased servicing by sub area
Estimate the flows the area would add and check capacity along the full path to treatment

tasks.explanation: Whole life cost matters because a cheap extension can saddle the utility with an expensive station forever. Connection standards at the start prevent the new area repeating the old areas problems.

tasks.prompt: Order the demand management options study for capacity relief.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian wastewater collection scenario for Class 4 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, provincial wastewater requirements in general terms, the federal Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations and the CCME Canada-wide Strategy as general references, and standard collection practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: before committing to a major trunk upsizing, leadership wants every demand side option tested on the same basis.

cards.label: Estimate the peak flow each option can remove or shift, using measured results from past programs where they exist
Recommend the portfolio and the point at which upsizing is still required, with that trigger stated as a flow or a date
Cost each option per unit of peak flow relieved using given rates so unlike options compare fairly
List the demand options, including I/I removal, water conservation effects on flow, storage, and development phasing
Monitor the delivered relief and report it against the forecast at each annual capacity review
Test the portfolio against the design events to confirm the combined effect meets the service level in the years claimed

tasks.explanation: Demand options only defer capital if their relief is measured, not hoped for. Stating the upsizing trigger in advance prevents the portfolio from becoming an excuse to defer forever.
